cse-2001-a-26.approach: Fix the units digit first (it decides evenness) and split on whether it is 0, because 0 cannot also be the leading digit.

steps.title: Units digit is 0
steps.body:
Thousands: any of $1$–$9$ (9 ways), hundreds: 8 left, tens: 7 left.

$$9 \times 8 \times 7 = 504$$

steps.title: Units digit is 2, 4, 6 or 8
steps.body:
4 choices for the units digit. Thousands: non-zero and not the units digit → $9 - 1 = 8$ ways. Hundreds: $10 - 2 = 8$ ways, tens: 7 ways.

$$4 \times 8 \times 8 \times 7 = 4 \times 448 = 1792$$

optionAnalysis.reason: 2240 undercounts; it does not match either case split.
2620 is not obtainable from the case split.
4536 counts all 4-digit numbers with distinct digits ($9\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7$), odd ones included.

Picking 2240 — that is the count of odd numbers.

cse-2001-a-27.approach: Each statement is existential, so one concrete example proves it.

steps.title: S1 by example
steps.body: Take $A = $ even integers, $B = C = $ odd integers. All three are infinite, but $A \cap (B \cup C) = \varnothing$, which is finite. S1 is true.

steps.title: S2 by example
steps.body: $x = \sqrt2$, $y = -\sqrt2$ are irrational, and $x + y = 0$ is rational. S2 is true.

answer.value: Both S1 and S2 are correct — option (C)

optionAnalysis.reason: S1 is also true (evens vs odds).

pitfalls: Assuming infinite sets must have an infinite intersection.
cse-2001-a-27.verification: Another S2 witness: $2-\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt2$ sum to 2.

cse-2001-a-28.approach: Images preserve unions exactly, but for intersections only $f(E\cap F) \subseteq f(E)\cap f(F)$ holds; a non-injective $f$ breaks equality.

steps.title: S1 holds
steps.body: $y \in f(E\cup F) \iff y = f(a)$ with $a \in E$ or $a \in F \iff y \in f(E) \cup f(F)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: S1 always holds; S2 fails for non-injective $f$.

pitfalls: S2 is true only when $f$ is injective — the question does not assume that.

cse-2001-a-29.approach: Each accident independently falls on one of 7 days; count favourable assignments over all assignments.

steps.title: Count outcomes
steps.body: Total assignments of 7 distinct accidents to 7 days: $7^7$. All on the same day: 7 ways (choose the day).

optionAnalysis.reason: $1/7^7$ fixes a particular day; any of the 7 days works.

pitfalls: Forgetting the factor 7 for the choice of the day.
cse-2001-a-29.verification: Equivalent view: the first accident picks the day, each of the other 6 matches it with probability $1/7$, giving $(1/7)^6$.

cse-2001-a-30.approach: Track (number of a mod 6, number of b mod 8); the product DFA has $6 \times 8$ states and all of them are pairwise distinguishable.

steps.title: Product DFA
steps.body: State $(i, j)$ with $i = \#a \bmod 6$, $j = \#b \bmod 8$; accept only $(0,0)$. That is $6 \times 8 = 48$ states.

steps.title: Minimality
steps.body: For $(i,j) \ne (i',j')$ append $a^{6-i}b^{8-j}$: it leads $(i,j)$ to $(0,0)$ (accept) but $(i',j')$ elsewhere (reject). So all 48 states are distinguishable.

optionAnalysis.reason: $6 + 8 = 14$ — counters add only for independent "or" style checks, not here.

pitfalls: Adding the moduli instead of multiplying.

cse-2001-a-31.approach: Check each language: $ww$ and $ww^R$ need unbounded memory, $0^{2i}$ is just even length, and $0^{i^2}$ has growing gaps between lengths.

steps.title: L1 and L2
steps.body: $L1 = \{ww\}$ is not even context-free; $L2 = \{ww^R\}$ (even palindromes) is context-free but not regular — pump $a^pbba^p$.

steps.title: Language L3
steps.body: $\{0^{2i}\}$ = strings of 0s of even length: a 2-state DFA accepts it. Regular.

steps.title: Language L4
steps.body: For $0^{p^2}$ pumping adds $k \le p$ symbols: $p^2 < p^2 + k < (p+1)^2 = p^2 + 2p + 1$, so the pumped length is not a square. Not regular.

optionAnalysis.reason: L1 and L2 are not regular.
L2 and L4 are not regular.

pitfalls: Mistaking $ww^R$ for regular because palindromes "look simple".
cse-2001-a-31.verification: Gaps between consecutive squares grow ($2i+1$), so no ultimately-periodic unary set equals L4.

cse-2001-a-32.approach: Reduce the halting problem to X (take q = the halting state); simulation gives a semi-decision procedure.

steps.title: Undecidable
steps.body: Given $(M, w)$, modify $M$ so every halting configuration first moves to a fresh state $q$. Then $M$ halts on $w$ iff the new machine visits $q$. A decider for X would decide halting.

steps.title: Partially decidable
steps.body: Simulate $M$ on $w$ step by step; if $q$ is entered, answer yes. This halts on every yes-instance, so X is recursively enumerable.

optionAnalysis.reason: Halting reduces to X, so it is not decidable.
It is a yes/no question, so it is a decision problem.

pitfalls: Confusing "not decidable" with "not even semi-decidable" — the complement (never visits q) is the non-r.e. one.
cse-2001-a-32.verification: Same structure as the state-entry problem in standard texts.

cse-2001-a-33.approach: Y = Q1 latches $X\cdot\overline{Q_0}$, so Y is a one-clock pulse after X is first sampled high. Since X rises exactly at an edge, the 20 ns setup time means that edge sees X = 0.
cse-2001-a-33.given:
| Signal | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $D_0 = X$ | $Q_0$ is X delayed by one clock |
| $D_1 = X\cdot\overline{Q_0}$ | $Y = Q_1$ |
| Setup | 20 ns, hold 0 |

steps.title: Edge 1 (X rises here)
steps.body: X changes at the edge itself, so it was not stable 20 ns before → both flip-flops sample $X = 0$. $Q_0 = 0$, $Y = 0$.

steps.title: Edge 2
steps.body: Before this edge $X = 1$, $\overline{Q_0} = 1$ → $D_1 = 1$. So $Y \to 1$ and $Q_0 \to 1$.

steps.title: Edge 3 onwards
steps.body: Now $\overline{Q_0} = 0$ → $D_1 = 0$ → $Y \to 0$, and stays 0 while X stays high (and after X falls, $D_1 = X\overline{Q_0} = 0$ anyway).

steps.title: Plot
steps.body: Y is high only between the 2nd and 3rd marked edges — the waveform in option (a).

answer.value: Y is high for one clock period, from the 2nd to the 3rd marked edge — option (A)

optionAnalysis.reason: Pulse from edge 2 to edge 3, as derived.
Starts at edge 1 — ignores the setup-time violation, and also lasts two periods instead of one.
Starts at edge 1 — ignores the 20 ns setup time.

pitfalls: Treating X as sampled high at the edge where it rises.
Forgetting that $\overline{Q_0}$ kills the AND one clock later.
cse-2001-a-33.verification: Circuit is a rising-edge detector: output pulse width is exactly one clock.

cse-2001-a-34.approach: Match each addressing mode to its classic use.

steps.title: Indirect and indexed
steps.body:
- Indirect: the parameter holds the address of the array, and the callee reaches the data through it → **passing array as parameter (III)**.
- Indexed: base address of the array + index register → **array implementation (I)**.

steps.title: Base register
steps.body: Addresses are offsets from a base register that the loader sets, so the program runs wherever it is loaded → **writing relocatable code (II)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: All three pairings are the standard uses.
Indirect addressing is not what makes code relocatable.
Indexed addressing serves arrays, base addressing relocation — swapped here.
Indirect is not the array-indexing mode.

pitfalls: Swapping base-register and indexed addressing.

cse-2001-a-38.approach: Count bus transfers (one per cycle on the single 8-bit bus) plus the 2-cycle memory write; the SP decrement is local and overlaps.

steps.title: Address into MAR
steps.body:
SP and MAR are 16-bit but the bus is 8-bit: the 8×(2:1) MUX and 8×(1:2) DEMUX move one byte per cycle.

Cycle 1: $\text{MAR}_{lo} \leftarrow \text{SP}_{lo}$; cycle 2: $\text{MAR}_{hi} \leftarrow \text{SP}_{hi}$.

steps.title: Data into MDR
steps.body: Cycle 3: $\text{MDR} \leftarrow r$ (same bus, so it cannot overlap cycles 1–2). SP can be decremented locally in this cycle — MAR already holds the old SP.

steps.title: Memory write
steps.body:
Cycles 4–5: $M[\text{MAR}] \leftarrow \text{MDR}$ (2 cycles).

$$2 + 1 + 2 = 5 \text{ cycles}$$

answer.keyNote: Stored key is B (3), but with an 8-bit bus the 16-bit SP needs 2 transfers to MAR, MDR ← r needs a third bus cycle, and the write itself takes 2 cycles: 5. Flagged for review.

optionAnalysis.reason: The memory write alone takes 2 cycles; loading MAR and MDR needs more.
3 cycles would need MAR and MDR loaded in one cycle, but the 8-bit bus carries only one byte per cycle.
4 assumes SP reaches MAR in one transfer, ignoring the 8-bit bus / byte MUX.
Two byte transfers for SP, one for r, two for the write.

pitfalls: Ignoring that SP is 16-bit while the bus is 8-bit.
Charging an extra cycle for SP ← SP − 1 — it is local.
cse-2001-a-38.verification: Lower bound: 3 bus transfers must precede the write, and the write is 2 cycles, so no schedule beats 5.

cse-2001-a-39.approach: BFS dequeues vertices in non-decreasing order of distance from r, but ties are possible.

steps.title: Order property
steps.body: BFS finishes all vertices at distance $k$ before any at distance $k+1$, so visiting u before v implies $d(r,u) \le d(r,v)$.

steps.title: Why not strict
steps.body: Two neighbours of r both have distance 1; one is visited first. So $<$ is not guaranteed.

optionAnalysis.reason: Fails for two vertices at the same level.
BFS never visits a farther vertex first.

pitfalls: Choosing strict inequality and forgetting ties within a level.

cse-2001-a-40.approach: A simple undirected graph on labelled vertices is any subset of the $\binom n2$ possible edges.

steps.title: Possible edges
steps.body: An undirected simple graph on the labelled set V is determined by its edge set, chosen from the $\binom n2 = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ unordered vertex pairs.

steps.title: Count subsets
steps.body: Each pair is present or absent independently: $2^{n(n-1)/2}$ graphs (the empty graph included, since connectivity is not required).

optionAnalysis.reason: That is the number of possible edges, not graphs.
Each of $n(n-1)/2$ edges is in or out.

pitfalls: Confusing number of edges with number of graphs.

cse-2001-a-41.approach: One stack reverses order, two reversals restore FIFO order.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body: Enqueue: push onto S1. Dequeue: if S2 is empty, pop everything from S1 and push onto S2; then pop S2. Elements leave in arrival order.

steps.title: One is not enough
steps.body: With one stack only the most recent element is accessible, but a queue must remove the oldest.

optionAnalysis.reason: A single stack gives LIFO order.

pitfalls: Thinking three are needed for "temporary" storage — S2 itself is the buffer.
cse-2001-a-41.verification: Enqueue 1,2,3 → S1 = [1,2,3]; transfer → S2 top is 1; dequeue gives 1.

cse-2001-a-42.approach: With call by reference, formal x aliases main's y, and formals y and z both alias main's x.

steps.title: Bindings
steps.body: `func1(y, x, x)`: formal `x` → main `y` (= 3); formal `y` and formal `z` → main `x` (= 10).

steps.title: y = y + 4
steps.body: Main `x` = 10 + 4 = 14 (seen through both `y` and `z`).

steps.title: z = x + y + z
steps.body: $3 + 14 + 14 = 31$ → main `x` = 31. Main `y` is untouched (3).

optionAnalysis.reason: 27 would use the old value 10 for one of the aliases; y never changes.

pitfalls: Missing that `y` and `z` are the same variable, so `z` already holds 14.

cse-2001-a-43.approach: Check where each returned pointer points: a dead stack frame, an uninitialised address, or valid heap memory.

steps.title: P1: address of a local
steps.body: Returns the address of local `x`, whose frame is gone after return → dangling pointer.

steps.title: P2: uninitialised pointer
steps.body: `px` is uninitialised; `*px = 10` writes to an arbitrary address → undefined behaviour.

steps.title: P3: heap memory
steps.body: `malloc` gives heap memory that outlives the call → safe (the caller should free it).

P3 is fine; P2 is broken.
P1 dangles, P2 writes through garbage.

cse-2001-a-44.approach: Inside D the name n refers to D's local n (3) under both scoping rules; W increments it by reference and prints it.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: Main sets global `n = 10`, calls `D`. D declares a local `n = 3` and calls `W(n)` — the argument is D's local n.

steps.title: Inside W
steps.body: `x` aliases D's n: `x = 3 + 1 = 4`; `print x` prints **4**. 4 is not among 10, 11, 3.

optionAnalysis.reason: 10 is the global n, which is never passed.
11 would mean the global n was incremented.
3 is the value before the increment.

pitfalls: Assuming dynamic scoping makes W use the global n — the argument is D's n either way.

cse-2001-a-45.approach: Interrupts are asynchronous hardware events; the scheduler is ordinary OS code that runs only after an interrupt or system call has already stopped the process.

steps.title: Hardware sources
steps.body: Devices raise I/O-completion interrupts; the timer raises the time-slice interrupt; power failure raises a high-priority (non-maskable) interrupt. All three are asynchronous signals to the CPU.

steps.title: The scheduler
steps.body: The scheduler is kernel code that runs only after an interrupt or system call has already stopped the process. It is a consequence of an interrupt, not a source of one.

optionAnalysis.reason: The scheduler is invoked by the kernel; it does not generate interrupts.

pitfalls: Thinking the scheduler preempts directly — it is the timer that does.

cse-2001-a-46.approach: Number of entries = virtual pages; entry size ≈ bits needed for a frame number.

steps.title: Entry size
steps.body: Frames $= 2^{26} / 2^{12} = 2^{14}$ → 14-bit frame number (plus a few flag bits) ≈ 2 bytes.

steps.title: Size
steps.body: $2^{20} \times 2\text{ B} = 2^{21}\text{ B} = 2\text{ MB}$.

cse-2001-a-47.approach: Process i waits only while j wants in and it is j's turn (i gave the turn away).

steps.title: Condition
steps.body: i sets `turn = j` politely. It must wait while `flag[j] == true` **and** `turn == j`.

steps.title: Why it works
steps.body: If both try, `turn` ends as whichever was written last; that process waits, the other enters. If j is not interested (`flag[j] = false`), i enters at once.

answer.value: flag[j] = true and turn = j — option (B)

flag[i] is always true here, so i would spin whenever it set turn = j: deadlock.
Tests i's own flag; does not guard against j.

pitfalls: Swapping the meaning of turn.

cse-2001-a-48.approach: Find the keys, then try BCNF decomposition; the classic failure is $AB \to C$, $C \to A$.

steps.title: Option (C)
steps.body: $AB \to C$, $C \to AD$. Keys: $AB$ and $BC$. $C \to AD$ violates BCNF (C is not a superkey). Any BCNF decomposition must separate $C$ from $AB$ (as $CAD$ and $CB$), losing $AB \to C$ — no lossless, dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition.

steps.title: Others work
steps.body: (A) $AB$, $BCD$. (B) $AB$, $BC$, $CD$. (D) $A$ is a key; R is already BCNF. All lossless and preserving.

cse-2001-a-50.approach: Deleting $(x,y)$ cascades to every tuple whose ub equals x, and recursively onward; follow the inequalities lb ≤ ub along the chain.

steps.title: Direct cascade
steps.body: Deleting $(x, y)$ removes lb value $x$, so every $(z, x)$ (ub $= x$) is deleted. In such tuples $z \le x$.

steps.title: Further cascade
steps.body: Deleting $(z, x)$ removes lb $z$, so tuples $(z', z)$ go too — here $w = z$, and $z$ can be $< x$. So a tuple with $w < x$ can be deleted.

steps.title: Rule out others
steps.body: Every deleted tuple $(z, w)$ satisfies $z \le w \le x \le y$, so $z > x$ or $z > y$ is impossible; cascade means deletion is allowed, not prohibited.

answer.value: A tuple $(z, w)$ with $w < x$ is deleted — option (C)

optionAnalysis.reason: Cascade deletes referencing rows instead of blocking.

pitfalls: Mixing up which column references which: ub references the primary key lb.
